goal: Ship and operate the status-page web service reliably with the staffing the team actually has (one person who can handle server upkeep, no on-call rotation), by choosing where to run it.
question: Select the deployment target for the status-page containerized web service: a managed platform that runs the container for the team, or a small self-managed virtual server that the team operates itself.
known_constraints: Budget supports either option: the README states the team can afford a managed platform or a small virtual server.
Operations staffing is one person who can handle server upkeep, and there is no on-call rotation.
The team has no strong preference between the two options yet.
The service is already containerized (Dockerfile based on python:3.12-slim) and listens on 0.0.0.0:8080.

environment.container: Docker image from python:3.12-slim, copies app.py, exposes port 8080
environment.statefulness: Stateless; no database, no external dependencies, no persistent storage
environment.service_behavior: Single HTTP handler returns 200 'status: ok' for every GET
environment.team_context: One person available for upkeep, no on-call rotation, no stated platform preference
environment.existing_deployment_automation: None found in the repository (no CI pipeline, no infrastructure-as-code, no TLS or ingress configuration)

evidence: app.py implements the whole service with Python's standard-library http.server (app.py:1-14): no third-party dependencies, no database, no persistent state, and it responds 200 'status: ok' to any GET on 0.0.0.0:8080.

app.py uses single-threaded HTTPServer rather than ThreadingHTTPServer (app.py:14), which is a development-grade server, so either target still relies on some outer layer (platform runtime or team-configured process manager) for restarts and robustness.

The Dockerfile builds from python:3.12-slim, copies app.py, and runs it as the image default user (Dockerfile:1-3); it defines no HEALTHCHECK and no non-root USER, so neither target inherits production hardening from the image itself.

README.md states verbatim: 'The team can afford either a managed platform or a small virtual server. One person can handle server upkeep, but there is no on-call rotation and no strong preference yet.' (English gloss: budget permits both options; a single person can maintain a server but nobody covers failures around the clock, and the team has no existing preference.)
The repository contains no CI pipeline, no infrastructure-as-code, no TLS or ingress configuration, and no deployment manifests, so deployment setup would be created from scratch under either option.

alternatives.name: Managed platform
alternatives.description: Deploy the existing container image to a managed container platform that runs it, restarts it, terminates TLS, and patches the underlying host.
advantages: The provider handles host patching, process restarts, and TLS termination, so no team time is spent on them.
Infrastructure failures are covered by the provider's staff, which compensates for the absence of an on-call rotation.
The existing container deploys as-is without the team building server provisioning, reverse proxy, or boot-time restart setup.
disadvantages: Recurring platform charges continue whether or not the service is being used.
Runtime behavior such as restart policy, logging, and metrics is expressed through the provider's abstractions.
Some provider-specific configuration would have to be rebuilt if the service moves elsewhere later.
assumptions: A managed container platform is available that accepts a python:3.12-slim image listening on port 8080.
The provider's achieved availability is at least as good as what one unassisted operator can sustain.

alternatives.name: Self-managed server
alternatives.description: Run the existing container image on a small virtual server that the team operates, with the team owning OS updates, TLS, and restart procedures.
advantages: Server cost is flat and predictable and the same machine can host other work later.
The team keeps full control over runtime configuration, networking, and the container environment.
Operational knowledge stays in-house instead of inside a provider's platform.
disadvantages: One person must perform OS patching, certificate renewal, and recovery with no on-call backup.
Server or container failures are noticed and fixed only when that single operator is available.
TLS, reverse proxy, and restart-on-reboot setup must be built and maintained by the team, since the repo contains none of it.
assumptions: A small virtual server can run the python:3.12-slim container and keep port 8080 reachable behind a proxy.
The single operator has the time and access to perform upkeep when it is needed.

criteria.name: Ongoing operational burden
rubric: Requires continuous after-hours coverage that the team does not have
Requires scheduled upkeep by one person, including patching, certificate renewal, and recovery
Requires only occasional review; restarts, patching, and TLS are covered by the platform or tooling
Requires essentially no ongoing upkeep beyond deploying changes

criteria.name: Availability of the status page itself
rubric: Single host with a single operator; outages persist until that person is available
Recovery depends on one person's response time, so brief unattended outages are likely
Managed restarts and host redundancy; outages are brief without team action
Independently hosted with managed multi-zone redundancy and health checks

criteria.name: Portability and lock-in
rubric: Runtime depends on provider-specific services that would need rework to leave
Runtime is portable but provider configuration such as DNS, TLS, and deploy settings would be rebuilt
Runtime is fully self-contained in the repository and runs unchanged anywhere Docker runs

criteria.name: Setup and change effort
rubric: Deployment must be designed and built from scratch, including TLS, proxy, and restart-on-reboot
Deployment is mostly configuration on top of an existing container workflow
Deploying a change is a single push of the existing image

criteria.name: Cost fit with the stated budget
rubric: Cost exceeds what the team stated it can afford
Cost is affordable but noticeably higher than the alternative
Cost is comparable to the affordable alternative
